chapters.name: Chapter 1: What AI can do for your business

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What AI is, in business terms
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Explain in your own words what an AI assistant can and cannot do for a business.
This lesson builds toward: In your own words, you will explain what an AI assistant can and cannot do for a business, including why the owner checks everything before it goes out.
An AI assistant is a computer program you type or talk to in everyday words. Well-known free ones include ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini. You ask for something, and it writes a draft in seconds.
For a business owner, think of it as a fast first-draft helper. It is good at writing emails, social posts and product descriptions, turning notes into a plan, summarizing long documents, brainstorming names and ideas, and explaining business words you do not know.
It is not your accountant, your lawyer or your customer. It does not know your prices, your customers or your local rules unless you tell it, and it can be wrong while sounding sure. You are the owner: you decide what goes out with your business name on it.
Words to know:
- AI assistant: a computer program you chat with by typing or talking, which writes answers and drafts.
- First draft: an early version of something that you will check and improve before using.
Try it now: Write down three things you did for your business last week that involved writing, planning or explaining. Circle the one that took you the longest.
You can now say what an AI assistant can do for a business, and why you still check everything before it goes out.

check.q: What does an AI assistant need from you to write about your business?
options: Your real prices, hours and details
Nothing; it already knows your business
check.why: AI does not know your business unless you tell it.

check.q: AI writes a flyer for your salon. What do you do before printing it?
options: Read and check it, because it goes out under your name
check.why: The owner is responsible for anything with the business name on it.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Finding the tasks AI can speed up
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List the tasks in your week that are good for AI, and the ones that are not.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of ten tasks from your week, you will sort your weekly business tasks into tasks AI can draft, tasks where AI helps you think, and tasks to keep for yourself, choosing one safe, useful first task for AI.
The best first tasks for AI are ones you repeat, that involve words, and where a mistake is easy to catch before anyone sees it. Examples: replying to common customer questions, writing a weekly post, drafting a flyer, making a checklist for a new helper, or summarizing a supplier's long email.
Tasks that are NOT good to hand to AI alone: anything that sends money, signs a contract, sets a legal or tax position, or makes a promise to a customer without you reading it first. AI can help you prepare, but you make the final call.
A simple way to sort: write each task on a line, then mark it "AI drafts, I check", "AI helps me think" or "I do it myself".
Step by step:
- List ten tasks you did in the last two weeks.
- Mark each one: AI drafts / AI helps me think / I do it myself.
- Pick the "AI drafts" task that takes you the most time.
- That is your first AI task.
Words to know:
- Repeat task: a job you do again and again, like answering the same customer question.
Try it now: Make your list of ten tasks and sort them into the three groups. Choose the one "AI drafts, I check" task you will use for the rest of this course.
You can now sort your business tasks and choose a safe, useful first task for AI.

check.q: What makes a task a good first task for AI?
options: It repeats, is mostly words and is easy to check
check.why: Repeated writing tasks that you can check easily are safe wins.

check.q: One task on your list is approving a supplier payment. How do you sort it?
check.why: Money decisions stay with the owner.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Writing a clear business prompt
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a three-part business prompt that gets a useful draft the first time.
This lesson builds toward: Given your chosen task, you will write a business prompt with a task, context and format, so the first draft is close to usable.
What you type to an AI assistant is called a prompt. A business prompt works best with three parts: the task, the business context, and the format you want.
Example: "Write a short welcome email for new customers of my home cleaning service in Atlanta. We clean homes every two weeks, and customers can text us to reschedule. Keep it friendly, under 120 words, with a clear subject line."
A weak prompt like "write an email" makes the assistant guess. It does not know your business, your customer or your tone, so the draft will be general. Never put customer names, phone numbers, card numbers or passwords into the prompt; you can add those yourself later.
Step by step:
- Task: say exactly what you want written or planned.
- Context: what you sell, who the customer is, where you are, your tone.
- Format: length, list or paragraphs, subject line, reading level.
- Read the prompt for private details and take them out before you send it.
Words to know:
- Prompt: what you type or say to an AI assistant to ask for something.
- Context: the background facts the AI needs, such as what you sell and who you sell to.
Try it now: Write a three-part prompt for the task you chose in Lesson 2. Send it to a free AI assistant and save the first draft.
You can now write a business prompt with a task, context and format, and leave private details out.

check.q: Which part of a business prompt is the format?
options: "We are a pet grooming shop in Phoenix"
check.why: Format says how you want the answer: length, layout or style.

check.q: Your prompt says only "write a post". What do you add?
options: Your business, your customers and how long and in what style you want it
check.why: Context and format turn a vague request into a useful draft.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Using AI safely and well

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Improving the draft with follow-ups
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Turn a first draft into a version you would really use, with follow-up requests.
This lesson builds toward: Given a first AI draft, you will ask follow-up requests, one at a time, and add your own real details, until it sounds like your business, in no more than three follow-ups.
The first answer is a draft. The assistant remembers the earlier messages in the same chat, so you can ask it to change one thing at a time.
Useful follow-ups for business writing: "Make it sound more like a small local business." "Cut it to 80 words." "Add a clear next step for the customer." "Give me three subject lines to choose from." "Write it at an easy reading level."
Add the facts only you know: your real hours, real prices and real policies. Then read it out loud. If it does not sound like you, ask for a change or edit it yourself.
Step by step:
- Read the first draft.
- Pick the one thing you most want changed.
- Ask for that change.
- Add your real facts.
- Read it out loud and repeat if needed.
Words to know:
- Follow-up: a second request in the same chat that changes or builds on the answer.
- Call to action: the clear next step you want the customer to take, like "Text us to book".
Try it now: Take your draft from Lesson 3. Ask for two changes, one at a time, then add your own real details. Compare the first and final versions.
You can now improve an AI draft with follow-ups and make it sound like your business.

options: A new chat about something else
A second request in the same chat that changes the answer
check.why: Follow-ups improve the draft you already have.

check.q: The draft is good but too long. What do you ask next?
options: Start over in a new chat
Ask for five more versions at once
check.why: One clear change at a time improves the draft.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Checking facts, numbers and claims
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check an AI draft for wrong facts, wrong numbers and promises you cannot keep.
This lesson builds toward: Given an improved draft, you will check every fact, number and claim against your own records or an official source, removing any claim you cannot prove.
AI can make things up: a price you never set, a rule that does not exist, a wrong total, or a claim like "the best in the city" that you cannot prove. Making things up like this is sometimes called a hallucination.
Before anything goes to a customer, check three things. Facts: hours, prices, addresses, policies. Numbers: do the totals and percentages add up? Do the math yourself or in a spreadsheet. Claims: can you prove it? In the United States the FTC says ads must be truthful, not misleading, and backed by evidence.
For tax, legal, licensing or money questions, use AI only to understand the words, then confirm with the official source (often a .gov site) or a professional such as an accountant or lawyer.
Step by step:
- Highlight every fact, number and claim in the draft.
- Check facts against your own records.
- Redo any math yourself.
- Remove or soften any claim you cannot prove.
- Confirm tax, legal or license points with an official source or a professional.
Words to know:
- Hallucination: when AI writes something that sounds true but is made up.
- Claim: something your business says is true, like "same-day service".
- FTC: the Federal Trade Commission, the US agency that enforces truth-in-advertising rules.
Official sources:
- FTC: Advertising and Marketing Basics
Try it now: Highlight every fact, number and claim in your improved draft. Check each one, fix what is wrong, and remove any claim you cannot prove.
You can now check an AI draft for wrong facts, wrong numbers and claims you cannot back up.

options: Something that sounds true but is made up
check.why: AI can write made-up facts that sound sure.

check.q: The draft says "rated number 1 in the city". You have no proof. What do you do?
options: Remove it or change it to something true
Ask AI if it is true
check.why: Advertising claims must be truthful and backed by evidence.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Protecting customer and business information
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI for business tasks without sharing private customer or money details.
This lesson builds toward: Whenever you use AI for the business, you will keep private customer and money details out of prompts and spot payment scams, using placeholders and sharing no card, bank or account numbers.
What you type into an AI chat may be stored by the company that runs it, and on some free plans it may be used to improve their AI. Read the tool's privacy settings, and assume anything you type could be seen by someone else.
Never type into an AI chat: customer names with phone numbers or addresses, card or bank numbers, passwords, Social Security or tax ID numbers, or private health details. Use placeholders such as "[customer name]" and fill them in yourself after.
Also watch for AI-powered scams aimed at businesses: fake invoices, emails that copy a supplier's style, and calls in a voice that sounds like someone you know asking for an urgent payment. Before paying, call back on a number you already know is real.
Step by step:
- Before sending a prompt, read it for private details.
- Replace them with placeholders like "[customer name]".
- Check the tool's privacy or data settings.
- Verify any urgent payment request by calling a number you already know.
Words to know:
- Placeholder: a stand-in like "[customer name]" that you replace with the real detail later, outside the AI chat.
- Invoice scam: a fake bill made to look like it comes from a real supplier.
Try it now: Final task: finish your chosen business task. Make sure the prompt and the final version have no private customer or money details, check every fact, number and claim, and save it ready to use.
You can now use AI for a real business task while protecting your customers, your money and your name.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Business prompt The prompt is vague, for example "write an email". The prompt has a task, context about the business and a format. It also names the customer and the goal, and the first draft is close to ready. Improved draft The first draft was used as it was. Two follow-up changes made, one at a time, plus the owner's own details. Can say what each change fixed, and the final version sounds like the business. Facts and claims checked A price, hour, total or claim was copied without checking. Every fact and number checked; every claim is true and provable. Notes where each fact was checked, and math was redone in a spreadsheet. Private details kept out The prompt or final version has card, bank or private customer details. No private customer or money details; placeholders used where needed. Also checked the AI tool's privacy setting for saving chats. Ready to use The final version is unfinished or not saved. Saved, checked and ready to use for the chosen task. Saved as a template the owner can reuse next time. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is a placeholder in a prompt?
options: A label like [customer name] instead of real details
check.why: Placeholders let you get help without sharing private details.

check.q: A message from your "bank" asks you to confirm your account number by reply. What do you do?
options: Ask AI to reply for you
Contact the bank using a number you already know
check.why: Use a contact you already trust, never the one in an urgent message.
